newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU finance ministers hold firm on strong lira.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers hold firm on strong lira.

text.p: European Union finance ministers and central bank governors played tough with Italy on Sunday, making clear they would not allow Rome to return to the EU's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) with a relatively weak lira.
Officials said Italy had trimmed earlier demands that it re-enter the grid at a central rate of 1,010 lira to the German mark, much weaker than ministers were ready to accept.
It was now willing to come in at 1,000 lira to the mark, they said, but the others had not accepted the deal and wanted a stronger rate for the currency.
"Other countries are seeking 950 to 980," a Spanish official said.

Some EU countries fear a too weak lira would give Italy preferential trade terms, but officials have also said the argument had implications for Rome's desire to be one of founding members of a future joint currency in Europe.

Sources said Germany, which is adamant that only strong economies should be given a chance to qualify for the planned single currency, was especially angry with Italy for seeking to re-enter the ERM at a weak rate.
"The Germans are not happy," one source said. Another said that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer wanted a rate of 970 liras to the mark.
The Bundesbank has been reluctant to accept that Italy, Spain and Portugal, with their relatively weak economies, could make it into the first wave of countries into the single currency.

The meeting on the issue dragged on into the evening, with some officials saying they expected it to go on for some hours. Few expected, however, that it would still be going on when foreign exchange makets opened in Asia on Monday.
Bank of England Governor Eddie George, who has no vote on the issue because Britain is not in the ERM, left early, saying he was sure there would be a decision on Sunday night.
Europe's top financial policy-makers had been called to Brussels after the EU's monetary committee of lower-level officials failed on Saturday to agree the terms for lira entry.

Luxembourg Finance Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, who is also the country's prime minister, said he was not surprised that the body had failed to agree because the issue had far-reaching political consequences.

"This is a political debate," he told reporters as he entered the meeting. "I don't think the monetary committee was the appropriate body for formulating an answer to a problem which is eminently political.
"The problem is whether or not we want to put Italy into a position where it fulfils one of the Maastricht criteria," he said.

Re-joining the ERM, from which the lira was unceremoniously dumped amid a currency crisis in 1992, is seen as crucial for Italy's hopes for being in the first wave of EU countries to adopt the single currency in 1999.
A stable two-year stint within the ERM -- designed to provide exchange rate stability -- is one of the qualifying criteria for the new currency, the Euro.
Italy, like other EU countries which want to join the monetary union from the start, has rushed to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, the budget deficit and public debt.
